title: Recursive CTEs: trees and graphs in SQL
goal: By the end, you can walk a chain of invitations of any length with one SQL query, carry each person's depth and path along the walk, stop the walk when the data loops back on itself, make a calendar of days out of nothing, and say which databases run the graph patterns of standard SQL in 2026.
opening:
Picture a café app that gives you a free coffee for inviting a friend. Asha invited Chloe and Elena, and each of them invited a friend. Now the company wants to thank Asha for her whole chain: everyone who joined through her, at any distance.

The first question people write for the database counts by levels: her friends, then her friends' friends, one more step for each level. It's right today, because no chain is longer than three invitations. Then someone at the bottom invites a friend, and the answer quietly leaves them out. It's an easy trap, because today's data seems to have fixed levels.

In Document stores with MongoDB, a refund went inside its payment's record, because it belongs to one payment. Invitations don't nest like that. In this lesson, we'll write a loop in SQL, the database's question language, that walks a chain of any length. We'll carry the path along, stop the loop when the data circles back, and meet SQL's newest graph patterns. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: We'll ask PostgreSQL, a database program, to repeat one step: "find the customers invited by the people we found last time". Nothing in the question says how many times. What makes PostgreSQL stop repeating?
options: A built-in limit of 100 repeats
A repeat that finds nobody at all
The first time it finds a customer it has already found
A LIMIT at the end of the query, which every query like this must have
warmup.why: PostgreSQL repeats the step, each time starting from the rows the last repeat found, and stops when a repeat finds no rows. There's no limit on the number of repeats. (SQL Server, Microsoft's database program, stops at 100 by default; PostgreSQL doesn't.) It doesn't watch for people it has already found, either. If the invitations ever loop back to someone, every round finds somebody, and the query runs until something cancels it. The third option is the tempting one, because it's what a careful person would do by hand. The database does it only when you ask, and the fourth section shows how.

sections.h: One join for every level, and why a chain of invitations needs a loop
sections.body:
Let's start with the data. The course database belongs to the payments company, and it runs on PostgreSQL, a free database program. It keeps its facts in tables, like sheets in a spreadsheet: each row is one record, and each column holds one kind of value. The `customers` table has 13 rows, one per customer. Its column `referred_by` holds the id of the customer who invited each one, or NULL when nobody did. NULL is the database's mark for "no value here". (Referred is the company's word for invited.)

Those pointers make a shape called a **tree**, because drawn out it branches like one. Each customer has at most one parent, the person who invited them, and any number of children, the people they invited. A customer with no parent is a **root**. The seed data, the rows the database starts with, has five roots: customers 1, 2, 7, 9 and 11. So it holds five separate trees, a **forest**, and two of them are a single customer. Asha (1) invited Chloe (3) and Elena (5). Chloe invited Farid (6), and Elena invited Jonas (10). A customer's **depth** is the number of steps down from their root, so Farid's is 2.

One level is easy. A query, a question written in SQL (the language people use to ask a database for data), asks for the customers whose `referred_by` is 1, and gets Chloe and Elena. The next level needs the customers whose inviter is one of those two. A **join** pairs the rows of two tables that match on some column. Here both sides are `customers`: each customer is paired with the row of the person who invited them. A join of a table with itself is a **self join**, from the SQL track's lesson "Joins, including semi and anti joins".

Each further level needs one more join. Ben (2) invited Daniel (4), who invited Hugo (8), who invited Mateo (13). Reaching Mateo from Ben takes two joins after the first level. Worse, the query must know the depth before it runs. The day Mateo invites someone, Ben's chain grows to four levels, and the two-join query misses the newcomer. There's no error, only a list that's one person short.

In Kotlin, you wouldn't write one statement per level. You'd write a loop:

```kotlin
var frontier = listOf(1L)                     // start from Asha
val downline = mutableListOf<Long>()
while (frontier.isNotEmpty()) {
    frontier = customers
        .filter { it.referredBy in frontier }     // one level down: what one self join does
        .map { it.id }
    downline += frontier
}
```

Each turn of the loop does the work of one self join. It finds the children of the customers the previous turn found, and they become the next `frontier`, the edge of what we've explored so far. The loop stops when a turn finds nobody. Nothing in it depends on how deep the tree is.

You could do the same with a phone. Call Asha and ask whom she invited. Then call each person she named and ask them. In each round, you only call the people you heard about in the round before, and you stop when a round of calls names nobody new.

That loop, written in SQL, is the picture for the rest of this lesson: **start somewhere, take one step from the rows you found last, and stop when a step finds nothing.** Next, we'll write it as one query.

aside.title: Why not run the loop in Kotlin, then?
aside.body: You can, and for a small tree it works. But the database is a separate program, and every question you send it is a trip there and back (SQL from the JVM: JDBC, pools, batching and migrations counted what those trips cost). A chain eight levels deep costs eight trips, and walking all 50,000 customers of the large data set means sending every row to your program first. A recursive query runs the whole loop inside the database, next to the data, as one statement. Each round is a join that the database plans like any other.

sections.h: WITH RECURSIVE: the loop, written as one query
sections.body:
Here's the Kotlin loop from the last section, written as one SQL statement:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE downline AS (
    SELECT customer_id, full_name, 0 AS depth          -- anchor: where the loop starts
    FROM customers
    WHERE customer_id = 1
  UNION ALL
    SELECT c.customer_id, c.full_name, d.depth + 1     -- recursive term: one level down
    FROM customers c
    JOIN downline d ON c.referred_by = d.customer_id
)
SELECT * FROM downline;
```

`WITH` gives a query a name inside a bigger statement. The named query is a **common table expression**, or CTE, from the SQL track's lesson "Subqueries and common table expressions". The rest of the statement can read it like a table. `WITH RECURSIVE` adds one thing: the named query may read itself.

The CTE has two parts. The first, the **anchor**, is an ordinary query that gives the starting rows: here, Asha at depth 0. The second, the **recursive term**, mentions the CTE's own name, `downline`. (Someone's downline is everyone below them in a chain like this.) That self-reference is what the word `RECURSIVE` allows, and it plays the part of `frontier` in the Kotlin loop. `UNION ALL` between the parts stacks their rows into one result, keeping any repeats.

PostgreSQL runs it with a **working table**, a scratch table that holds the rows of the latest round:

1. Run the anchor. Put its rows in the result and in the working table.
2. Run the recursive term. Wherever it says `downline`, read only the working table. Add the new rows to the result, and make them the new working table.
3. Repeat step 2 until a round produces no rows.

The working table is the list of people you heard about in the last round of phone calls. For Asha, the anchor gives {1}. Round 1 joins customers to {1} and finds {3, 5}. Round 2 joins them to {3, 5} and finds {6, 10}. Round 3 joins them to {6, 10}, finds nobody, and the loop ends with five rows. The stepper below runs the same loop over the whole forest. Despite the name, nothing calls itself: the PostgreSQL documentation calls this iteration, and the three steps above are a while loop.

Two things follow from the way it runs. First, the recursive term only ever sees the latest round, never the whole result so far, so it can't count or add up. Put `count(*)` in it and PostgreSQL refuses: `aggregate functions are not allowed in a recursive query's recursive term`. Count in the main query, after the loop. Second, there's no built-in limit. The loop stops when a round comes back empty, and only then. SQL Server, Microsoft's database program, stops after 100 levels by default. PostgreSQL doesn't, so data that never runs out of new rows gives a query that never ends. The fourth section deals with that.

Each round is an ordinary join, planned like any other. On a larger copy of the data, with 50,000 customers, the whole forest comes out in 8 rounds and about 40 ms. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, which runs a query and prints the steps PostgreSQL took, shows the loop: a step called `WorkTable Scan` reads the working table, and its `loops=8` counts the rounds. Lesson 9 meets this loop again under another name.

The same loop can make rows out of nothing. A report for March needs one row per day, quiet days included. GROUP BY, which folds rows into one line per group, can't invent a day that has no payments. A recursive CTE can. The anchor is `SELECT date '2026-03-01' AS day`. The recursive term is `SELECT day + 1 FROM days WHERE day < date '2026-03-31'`, and the round after 31 March is empty because its WHERE turns false. Then LEFT JOIN the payments to the days, so that every day stays, with or without a payment. Put the payment conditions in ON, the part of a join that says which rows match, and count `p.payment_id` rather than `*`, so an empty day counts 0, not 1. PostgreSQL code usually uses its function `generate_series` for this, and the recursive form also works in other databases.

The loop finds everyone, but in the order the rounds found them. Next, we'll print a tree the way people draw one.

sections.h: Carrying the path down the walk, and printing the tree in order
sections.body:
The rows of a recursive CTE come out round by round: 1, then 3 and 5, then 6 and 10. Like any query result, they have no order you can rely on unless you ask for one. Round by round is called **breadth-first** order: the whole first level, then the whole second. To print the tree with each customer indented under the person who invited them, you want 1, 3, 6, 5, 10. That goes down one branch to the bottom before it starts the next. It's called **depth-first** order, and you need something to sort by.

A column worked out in the recursive term is carried down the tree, round after round. `d.depth + 1` already does that for the depth. Do the same with the **path**, the list of ids from the root down to the row:

```sql
SELECT customer_id, 0 AS depth, ARRAY[customer_id] AS path ...      -- anchor
SELECT c.customer_id, d.depth + 1, d.path || c.customer_id ...      -- recursive term
```

`ARRAY[customer_id]` builds an array, a list of values held in one column, with one element in it. `||` adds an element to its end, so Farid's path is `{1,3,6}`. PostgreSQL compares two arrays element by element, the way a dictionary compares words letter by letter. So `ORDER BY path` puts `{1,3}` and `{1,3,6}` before `{1,5}`, which is depth-first. The path answers other questions too. `path[1]` is the root of the row's tree (PostgreSQL counts array elements from 1), and `cardinality(path) - 1`, the number of elements minus one, is the depth.

PostgreSQL 14 added a standard clause that builds the sort key for you. Write `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY customer_id SET ord` right after the CTE's closing bracket, and every row gets an extra column, `ord`. `ORDER BY ord` in the main query then sorts depth-first, and `SEARCH BREADTH FIRST BY customer_id SET ord` sorts by round. The hand-made path works on every version, and you can read it. SEARCH is shorter.

The same loop walks up the tree. Flip the join: start from Mateo, and join each row to the person who invited them, `c.customer_id = u.referred_by`. The loop visits 13, 8, 4 and 2, and stops at Ben, whose `referred_by` is NULL. A comparison with NULL is never true (the SQL track's first lesson, "The relational model, keys and NULL"), so that round finds nothing. Walking up is cheap, because each round finds at most one row: nobody has more than one inviter.

So far the data has been a tree, and every walk ended by itself. Next, we'll break that on purpose.

sections.h: When the data loops back: cycles, and three ways to stop the walk
sections.body:
In real life, a chain of invitations can't loop: Farid can't have invited Asha, who joined before him. The table refuses a customer who invited themselves, but it can't see longer loops. So nothing stops an UPDATE, a statement that changes a row, from recording Asha as invited by Farid, two levels below her. Then the chain goes 1, 3, 6, 1, 3, 6, and the walk from the second section never ends. Round 3 finds Asha again, round 4 finds Chloe and Elena again, and the working table is never empty.

On the phone, it's the moment Farid says he invited Asha. If you call everyone you're told about, you'll call the same three people forever. That's where the phone picture breaks, too: a person would notice the repeat, and PostgreSQL doesn't. In practice, someone fixes a record by hand, and two rows end up pointing at each other. A query that worked for months then runs until something cancels it, or until it fills the disk with its own rows. The Try it below makes this loop on purpose.

A tree is a special kind of **graph**. A graph is any set of things, called **nodes**, joined by links, called **edges**. In general, the edges can form a **cycle**: a path that comes back to where it started. Money makes a graph full of cycles. The course database keeps a ledger, a record of every movement of money from one account to another. Farid's account 106 paid Volt Electronics, a shop with account 304, and Volt refunded account 106. Any query that follows money has to expect cycles.

There are three ways to make the loop stop.

The first is `UNION` instead of `UNION ALL`. UNION drops every new row that equals a row already in the result. If each row holds only the node's id, that works as a list of visited nodes: a node found once is never added again, so the loop ends. But add a depth or a path column, and two visits to the same node are no longer equal rows. UNION then drops nothing, and the loop runs on.

The second is to carry the path and refuse to step onto a node that's already on it: `WHERE c.customer_id <> ALL (d.path)` in the recursive term, which reads "the new id differs from every id on the path".

The third is to let PostgreSQL 14 or later keep that list for you. Write `CYCLE customer_id SET is_cycle USING path` after the closing bracket. It adds two columns: `path`, the nodes visited so far, and `is_cycle`, true or false. A row whose node is already on its path comes out once with `is_cycle` true, and the walk doesn't follow it further. Filter it out with `WHERE NOT is_cycle` in the main query.

**Data that people can edit will one day loop. Guard every walk over it.** A CYCLE clause costs little, and a time limit on the query is a second guard.

The path methods have a limit. They stop a cycle along one path, but they don't remember nodes that another path reached. So the same account can show up several times, once for each route to it, and in a graph with many links the number of routes grows fast. If you need each node once, with its shortest distance, group after the loop: `GROUP BY account_id` with `min(hops)`. The lab's money walk needs exactly that.

DuckDB, a small database program built for analysis, cuts that repeated work inside the loop. Since version 1.3 (May 2025), a recursive CTE there can say `USING KEY (account_id)`. The result then keeps one row per account, like a map. A new row for an account replaces the old one instead of being added, so the result never grows past the number of accounts. It's DuckDB's own extension, not standard SQL, and PostgreSQL has nothing like it.

Paths, cycle checks and shortest distances are a lot of bookkeeping for one question. Next, we'll see standard SQL move it into the database.

sections.h: Graph patterns in standard SQL, and who runs them in 2026
sections.body:
A recursive CTE spells out every step as a join and leaves the bookkeeping to you. SQL has a standard, a rulebook for the language that ISO, the international standards body, publishes every few years. Database programs follow it to different degrees. Its 2023 edition, SQL:2023, added a new part for graphs, SQL/PGQ (property graph queries). It brings two things.

The first is `CREATE PROPERTY GRAPH`. A property graph is a graph whose nodes and edges carry named values, such as an account's id; lesson 8 opens it up. The statement says which existing tables hold the nodes, which hold the edges, and which columns connect them. Nothing is copied. The graph is only a definition over the tables, like a view, a saved query you can read as if it were a table. Say the ledger's money movements are available as a view `transfers(journal_id, from_account, to_account)`, one row per movement:

```sql
CREATE PROPERTY GRAPH money
VERTEX TABLES (
    accounts
)
EDGE TABLES (
    transfers
        SOURCE KEY (from_account) REFERENCES accounts (account_id)
        DESTINATION KEY (to_account) REFERENCES accounts (account_id)
);
```

`VERTEX TABLES` lists the tables of nodes (vertex is another word for node), and `EDGE TABLES` the tables of links, with the column at each end.

The second is `GRAPH_TABLE`. It matches a pattern drawn with brackets and arrows, the style lesson 8 uses, and returns an ordinary table that you can join and add up like any other:

```sql
FROM GRAPH_TABLE (money
    MATCH p = ANY SHORTEST (a:accounts)-[t:transfers]->{1,6}(b:accounts)
    WHERE a.account_id = 106
    COLUMNS (b.account_id AS account_id, path_length(p) AS hops)
);
```

Read the pattern as a picture: an account `a`, an arrow that is a transfer, and another account `b`. `{1,6}` repeats the arrow one to six times, and `ANY SHORTEST` keeps one shortest path to each account. That's the lab's money walk: up to six transfers out of account 106, with each account it reaches listed once, with its fewest hops. `ANY SHORTEST` does the job that the CYCLE clause and `min(hops)` did by hand.

Who runs it, as of November 2026? Oracle does. Oracle is a commercial database that many large companies run, and Oracle Database 23ai was the first commercial system with SQL/PGQ. Its newer release, Oracle AI Database 26ai, builds property graphs over tables, views and even columns of JSON, a text format for nested data. Spanner Graph, the graph side of Google's cloud database Spanner, does too, and it also speaks GQL, the graph language standard that lesson 8 meets. DuckDB does, through `duckpgq`, a community extension (an add-on that users install) from the CWI research institute in Amsterdam: `INSTALL duckpgq FROM community; LOAD duckpgq;`, plus `SET active_grammar_extensions = ['duckpgq'];` on DuckDB 2.0. The queries above use its syntax.

PostgreSQL doesn't. SQL/PGQ was announced in the first beta (test release) of PostgreSQL 19 in June 2026 and taken out again in the fourth, so 19 ships without it. Graph queries on PostgreSQL today mean Apache AGE, an add-on that speaks Cypher, the language lesson 8 teaches. In a 2024 survey of data models, the database researchers Michael Stonebraker and Andrew Pavlo cite DuckPGQ beating a leading graph database by up to ten times. That's their main reason to doubt that graphs need a database of their own.

Next, Graph databases with Neo4j and Cypher makes the case for one.

What's left for you is the pattern. The bookkeeping moves into the database, which is free to run a graph search instead of joins round by round.

compare.title: Walking a chain: Oracle's CONNECT BY and PostgreSQL's WITH RECURSIVE

a.label: Oracle
a.title: Oracle CONNECT BY
a.src:
-- Oracle's own hierarchical syntax
SELECT customer_id,
       LEVEL - 1                             AS depth,
       SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH(customer_id, '/') AS path
FROM customers
START WITH customer_id = 1
CONNECT BY NOCYCLE PRIOR customer_id = referred_by
ORDER SIBLINGS BY customer_id;
-- without NOCYCLE a loop raises
-- ORA-01436: CONNECT BY loop in user data

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL 18
b.src:
WITH RECURSIVE downline AS (
    SELECT customer_id, 0 AS depth, ARRAY[customer_id] AS path
    FROM customers WHERE customer_id = 1
  UNION ALL
    SELECT c.customer_id, d.depth + 1, d.path || c.customer_id
    FROM customers c
    JOIN downline d ON c.referred_by = d.customer_id
) CYCLE customer_id SET is_cycle USING cycle_path
SELECT customer_id, depth, path
FROM downline
WHERE NOT is_cycle
ORDER BY path;
-- without CYCLE a loop runs until statement_timeout

compare.note: Both list Asha's chain depth-first. Oracle has its own older syntax for this walk. `START WITH` is the anchor. `CONNECT BY PRIOR customer_id = referred_by` is the recursive join, and `PRIOR` marks the column of the parent row, the one found in the step before. `LEVEL` is the depth, counted from 1, and `SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH` builds the path as text. PostgreSQL never had CONNECT BY, so Oracle queries that use it must be rewritten when they move. Oracle has also understood the standard recursive WITH since version 11g Release 2, with small differences: no RECURSIVE keyword, a list of column names after the CTE's name, UNION ALL only, and its own SEARCH and CYCLE clauses. The biggest difference is the cycle. Oracle notices one and raises an error unless you ask for NOCYCLE or CYCLE. PostgreSQL doesn't notice one at all unless you write CYCLE or a path check, and keeps running.

worked.title: Everyone's whole chain, counted in one statement

steps.say: The company now wants a number for every customer: how many people joined anywhere below them, and how many they invited themselves. A walk down from one customer answers for that one. To answer for all of them, start a walk from every customer at once, and carry the starting customer down as a column. The anchor makes each customer their own `ancestor_id` (an ancestor is anyone above you in the chain), at depth 0.
steps.code:
-- 1. anchor: every customer starts a walk of its own
WITH RECURSIVE below AS (
    SELECT customer_id AS ancestor_id, customer_id, 0 AS depth
    FROM customers

steps.say: The recursive term steps down one level and copies `ancestor_id` unchanged, the way the third section carried the path. Each row of the result now says "this customer is below that ancestor, at this depth". There's one row for each (ancestor, descendant) pair, plus the 13 rows at depth 0: 26 rows in all.
steps.code:
-- 2. recursive term: one level down, same ancestor
  UNION ALL
    SELECT b.ancestor_id, c.customer_id, b.depth + 1
    FROM customers c
    JOIN below b ON c.referred_by = b.customer_id
)

steps.say: The recursive term can't count, so count in the main query, after the loop. FILTER (from the SQL track's lesson "Aggregation: GROUP BY, FILTER, ROLLUP and GROUPING SETS") counts only the rows that pass its condition, so one group gives both the whole chain and the direct invitations. HAVING, a WHERE for groups, drops the customers who invited nobody.
steps.code:
-- 3. aggregate after the loop
SELECT b.ancestor_id, cu.full_name,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE b.depth > 0) AS downline,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE b.depth = 1) AS direct,
       max(b.depth)                        AS levels
FROM below b
JOIN customers cu ON cu.customer_id = b.ancestor_id
GROUP BY b.ancestor_id, cu.full_name
HAVING count(*) FILTER (WHERE b.depth > 0) > 0
ORDER BY downline DESC, b.ancestor_id;

steps.say: Check it against the forest. Asha has 4 below her (3, 5, 6 and 10), and invited two of them herself. Ben has 3, in a chain three levels deep. Daniel, in the middle of Ben's chain, has 2. Seven customers invited someone, which matches the seed data: everyone except 6, 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13.

lab.title: A forest of any depth, a money graph with cycles, and a calendar
steps: With Docker running, run the tests from the `labs` folder. All six fail. The tests cancel any statement after 10 seconds, so a loop that never ends fails its test instead of hanging.
`referral_tree.sql` stops after one self join. Rewrite it with WITH RECURSIVE so it returns every customer with `root_id` (the root of their tree), `depth` and `path`, in path order.

`money_reach.sql` walks the money graph from account 106 with a depth cap that hides the cycles. Remove the cap, make the walk stop on its own, and return each account it reaches once, with its fewest hops.
`daily_volume_march.sql` misses the quiet days. Make the 31 days of March first, then LEFT JOIN the succeeded payments to them.
Run the tests until all six pass. Each exercise has a second test that adds rows first: a deeper chain, a new transfer, payments right at the edges of a day.
hints: Carry `root_id` down unchanged in the recursive term, the way the worked example carries `ancestor_id`. The anchor sets it to the root's own id.
Add `CYCLE account_id SET is_cycle USING path` after the `reach` CTE's closing bracket. Then keep only `NOT is_cycle` and `account_id <> 106`, and `GROUP BY account_id` with `min(hops)`.
Count `p.payment_id`, not `*`, and put `p.status = 'succeeded'` in the ON clause. A day is `p.created_at >= d.day AND p.created_at < d.day + 1`.

drill.title: A walk that survives cycles, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write a recursive CTE that lists everyone below Ben (customer 2), with their depth and their path of ids. Protect it against cycles with a path check (no CYCLE clause), and sort it depth-first. Then say in which round it stops on the seed data, and why.

answer.src:
WITH RECURSIVE downline AS (
    SELECT customer_id, 0 AS depth, ARRAY[customer_id] AS path   -- anchor: Ben
    FROM customers
    WHERE customer_id = 2
  UNION ALL
    SELECT c.customer_id, d.depth + 1, d.path || c.customer_id    -- one level down
    FROM customers c
    JOIN downline d ON c.referred_by = d.customer_id
    WHERE c.customer_id <> ALL (d.path)                           -- never revisit a node on this path
)
SELECT customer_id, depth, path
FROM downline
WHERE depth > 0
ORDER BY path;
-- 4 {2,4}, 8 {2,4,8}, 13 {2,4,8,13}.
-- Round 4 starts from {13}, finds nobody with referred_by = 13, and is empty: the loop stops.

recap: A self join climbs one level per join, so it needs the depth before it runs, and it misses anyone deeper without an error. A recursive CTE is the loop that doesn't.

`WITH RECURSIVE` runs the anchor once, then runs the recursive term on the previous round's rows (the working table) until a round produces nothing. A WHERE in the recursive term can end it too, which is how a calendar of days is made.
Carry columns down the walk: `depth + 1`, a path array built with `||`, a root id. Sort by the path, or use SEARCH DEPTH FIRST, to print a tree in order. Count after the loop, never inside it.

PostgreSQL has no depth limit and doesn't notice cycles. Stop them with the CYCLE clause, a path check, or UNION on rows that hold only the node id. DuckDB's USING KEY keeps one row per key inside the loop.

SQL/PGQ, part of SQL:2023, adds CREATE PROPERTY GRAPH over existing tables and GRAPH_TABLE to match patterns. In November 2026 it runs in Oracle 23ai and 26ai, Spanner Graph and DuckDB's duckpgq, not in PostgreSQL.

The limit: a path check stops loops, not repeated work. Every route to a node is walked on its own, and in a graph with many links the routes multiply at each step, so cap the depth or let the database search for shortest paths.
closing:
We started with a thank-you for Asha's whole chain, and a query that would have missed the next person to join. The loop has no depth written into it: it steps from the last round's rows and stops when a step finds nobody. That's also why a chain that loops back needs a guard.

In psql, run `\d customers` and find the line where `referred_by` references `customers` itself. A column that points back at its own table is a tree, or a graph, waiting for a recursive query.

Next, we'll keep links like these in a database built for them, and find out why each extra step costs tables more joins but a graph store only a short hop.

quiz.q: Mateo (13) invites a new customer, Nia (14). What must change in the recursive query that lists everyone below Ben (2), so that it includes her?
options: Nothing: one more round finds her
The anchor, so that it starts from 13
A fourth self join in the recursive term
The depth limit in the query
quiz.why: The recursive term finds the children of whatever the last round found. So the round that starts from {13} now finds Nia, and the round after it is empty. That's the point of the loop: the depth isn't written into the query. A fixed chain of self joins would need a fourth join, and there's no depth limit to raise.

quiz.q: A recursive CTE has the columns (account_id, hops) and uses UNION instead of UNION ALL. The money graph has a cycle. What happens?
options: It stops: UNION removes accounts it has already seen
It raises a cycle error
It runs until a time limit stops it: hops is different on every visit, so no row is ever an exact repeat
It returns only the first round
quiz.why: UNION drops a new row only when the whole row equals one already found. Each trip round the cycle adds 1 to hops, so the rows never match, and every round has new ones. UNION works as a list of visited nodes only when a row holds the node id alone, which is why the first option is so tempting. Use CYCLE or a path check instead, then min(hops) after the loop.

quiz.q: Your team wants to run SQL/PGQ queries (`GRAPH_TABLE ... MATCH`) on its real data in November 2026. Which of these can run them?
options: PostgreSQL 18, through a built-in GRAPH_TABLE function
PostgreSQL 19, which shipped SQL/PGQ
Oracle AI Database 26ai
None yet: SQL/PGQ is only a draft standard
quiz.why: SQL/PGQ is part 16 of SQL:2023, a published standard. Oracle has run it since 23ai, and so do Spanner Graph and DuckDB, through the duckpgq extension. PostgreSQL 19's first beta announced it, but the fourth beta took it out again, so neither 18 nor 19 has it. On PostgreSQL, graph queries mean the Apache AGE add-on and the Cypher language.

quiz.q: You want the size of each root's whole tree. Where does `count(*)` go?
options: In the recursive term, to count each round
In the anchor
In the main query after the CTE, grouped by a root id carried down the walk
Nowhere: a recursive CTE can't be counted
quiz.why: The recursive term sees only one round, and PostgreSQL refuses to count there. Carry the root's id down unchanged, then `GROUP BY root_id` in the main query, where every row of the walk exists.

quiz.q: From Document stores with MongoDB: a payment's refunds fit well inside the payment's own document, one record that holds everything about it. Why not store the forest of invitations the same way, with the people each customer invited nested inside that customer's document?
options: MongoDB can't store lists inside lists
Fields inside a document can't be indexed
MongoDB's 16 MB limit applies to each item of a list
Refunds are few and belong to one parent. A chain has no depth limit and everyone in it is both a child and a parent, so nesting copies each branch into every ancestor and grows without bound
quiz.why: That lesson put things inside one document when they're read together, changed together and few in number. A tree of invitations is none of those. Mateo would sit inside Hugo's, Daniel's and Ben's documents, so one new invitation changes every ancestor, and the depth has no limit. Store one link per row or document and follow the links, which is this lesson. Lists inside lists and indexes on nested fields both work fine in MongoDB.

flashcards.front: What are the two parts of a recursive CTE?
flashcards.back: The anchor, which runs once and gives the starting rows, and the recursive term, which mentions the CTE's own name. UNION or UNION ALL joins them.

flashcards.front: When the recursive term mentions the CTE's name, what does it read?
flashcards.back: Only the working table: the rows the previous round produced, not the whole result so far.

flashcards.front: When does a recursive CTE stop in PostgreSQL?
flashcards.back: When a round produces no rows. There's no depth limit.

flashcards.front: How do you print a tree depth-first from a recursive CTE?
flashcards.back: Carry a path array (`path || id`) and ORDER BY path, or add `SEARCH DEPTH FIRST BY id SET ord` and ORDER BY ord.

flashcards.front: What does `CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path` do?
flashcards.back: Keeps the ids on each path, marks a row that comes back to one of them with is_cycle = true, and doesn't follow that row further.

flashcards.front: When does UNION (not UNION ALL) stop a cycle?
flashcards.back: Only when each row holds only the node id, so a second visit is an exact repeat. A depth or path column defeats it.

flashcards.front: Which databases run SQL/PGQ (GRAPH_TABLE) queries in November 2026?
flashcards.back: Oracle (23ai and 26ai), Google Spanner Graph, and DuckDB through the duckpgq extension. Not PostgreSQL: it was taken out of PostgreSQL 19's betas.

terms.plain: Rows linked by a pointer to a parent, each with at most one parent, like customers and the people who invited them. A root has no parent.
Things (nodes) joined by links (edges) in any pattern. A cycle is a path of links that comes back to where it started.
The first part of a recursive CTE, an ordinary query. It runs once and gives the starting rows.
The part after UNION ALL that mentions the CTE's own name. It runs once per round and gives the next round's rows.
The rows the latest round produced. The next round of the recursive term reads only these.
The list of ids from the start of the walk down to the current row, carried along as an array.
PostgreSQL 14 and later: keeps the path of each row, and stops following a row that comes back to a node already on it.
Part 16 of the SQL:2023 standard: CREATE PROPERTY GRAPH over existing tables, and GRAPH_TABLE to match graph patterns inside a query.

explain_back.prompt: A shop chain keeps its regions and stores in one table, each row pointing at the region above it. A nightly job lists every store under each region with a recursive CTE. After a big import of new rows, the job stopped finishing. Explain what most likely happened, why PostgreSQL didn't stop on its own, and how you'd make the query safe.
explain_back.answer: A recursive CTE stops only when a round produces no rows. The import most likely made a cycle, for example a region whose parent is one of its own stores. Then every round keeps finding rows, and the working table is never empty. PostgreSQL has no depth limit and doesn't look for cycles, and UNION ALL keeps every repeated row, so the job runs until a time limit stops it or the disk fills. To make it safe, add `CYCLE store_id SET is_cycle USING path` after the CTE (or carry a path array and skip ids already on it), keep only `NOT is_cycle` in the main query, and set a `statement_timeout` for the job. Then find the bad rows: the ones with `is_cycle` true name them. If the data must be a tree, also refuse cycles when rows are written.

deeper.body:
A recursive CTE works the tree out again on every query. That's fine for a forest of 50,000 customers (about 40 ms). But if a tree is read far more often than it changes, you can store it in a form that needs no loop to read. There are three classic designs:

- An **adjacency list** is what `customers.referred_by` is: one pointer to the parent in each row. Writes are easy, and reads need the loop.
- A **closure table** stores every (ancestor, descendant, depth) pair as a row of its own. The worked example worked out exactly that table, 26 rows for this forest. Reading a whole chain becomes `WHERE ancestor_id = 2`, one quick lookup in an index. But adding a customer means adding one row per ancestor, and moving a branch touches many rows.
- A **materialized path** stores the path in each row, like `{2,4,8,13}`, so "everyone below 4" becomes a test of how the path starts. PostgreSQL ships the `ltree` extension for paths of this kind, with an index type (GiST) that serves those tests.

The CYCLE clause and the path array both keep a separate path for each route, so they stop cycles but not repeated work. In the money graph, the walk from account 106 produced 12 rows for 6 accounts, because several routes reach the same account. In a graph with many links, the number of routes that never repeat a node grows exponentially with the depth, since each step multiplies it. So a walk that's safe from cycles can still take forever. Cap the depth as well (`WHERE r.hops < 6`) when you only care about nearby nodes. Or use UNION with rows that hold only the node id, which gives a true list of visited nodes, and work out the distances separately.

DuckDB's `USING KEY`, from the fourth section, has one more part. Inside the loop, the recursive term can also read the whole result so far, under the name `recurring.reach`, and not only the last round.

Finally, a recursive CTE stores every round's rows before the main query reads them, so a walk that finds millions of rows spills to disk like any other large result in the middle of a query. On the large data set, the forest walk kept its 50,000 rows in about 2.4 MB of memory (`Storage: Memory  Maximum Storage: 2419kB` on the Recursive Union step of the plan).
